title: Pressure Gradient Wind Map
creator: Hank R. & Claude Code
subject: Environmental Monitoring
description: An analytic isobar field where a deep low blows a gentle breeze and a shallow one blows a near gale, so the gradient rather than the central pressure becomes the readable signal.

learningObjectives: Examine an isobar map and predict wind speed and direction at any point.
Differentiate the effect of gradient steepness from the effect of absolute pressure.
Explain why surface air crosses isobars at an angle instead of flowing straight downhill.
Locate the strongest wind on a chart from isobar spacing alone.
prerequisites: Chapter 10: pressure systems, fronts and the Coriolis effect

keyQuestions: Which is the better predictor of wind: how low the pressure is, or how fast it changes with distance?
Why does the wind not blow straight from high pressure to low pressure?
Where on a chart with a high and a low next to each other would you expect the strongest wind?
What changes about the wind when a cold front passes over you?
commonMisconceptions: Low central pressure always means strong wind.
Wind blows directly downhill from high pressure to low pressure.
Strong winds only happen around low pressure systems.
The windiest place on a chart is at a pressure centre.
assessmentOpportunities: Ranks two maps by wind speed using isobar spacing rather than central pressure.
Predicts wind direction, including the Coriolis deflection, for a given hemisphere.
Scores above 80 per cent of the map maximum in the hidden-arrow prediction mode.
